title: Who Owns What: Organizing Marketplace Engineering
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the organizing-marketplace-engineering entry in journal-spec.json; the supporting claims, audience and AC-4/AC-5 are this spec's own. Units added by this conversion: introduction roadmap p04, lead-ins p56 (Trade-offs), p57 (Vertical Differences), the lead sentences of p59 and p65, and a conclusion widened to two paragraphs (p66 synthesis and callback, p67 hand-off).

know: Conway's law as a design tool; the four team types and three interaction modes, and the marketplace team topology that assigns them to journeys, bounded contexts and shared capabilities.

Platform teams as internal products (team API, contract, roadmap, migration help), decision rights across group, platform and brand, the advice process and its forum, funding models by phase, and the roles of architects.
believe: Ownership is the unit of design: a capability exists as many times as there are teams that believe they own it.
A platform team earns its tenants; adoption by mandate without a contract produces shadow copies.

audience.who: Chief and enterprise architects, CTOs, heads of platform engineering and engineering directors of marketplace groups, especially after acquisitions.

From earlier chapters: the capability map (business-capabilities), the context map and one owning team per bounded context (bounded-contexts), the tenancy model and the March 2027 phishing rule (multi-country-platforms, trust-and-safety-architecture), the search platform and Listing Search API v1 (search-architecture), ranking (ranking), Tally (products-and-entitlements), the ML platform (ml-platform), the bikes split (categories-and-taxonomies), and platform-consolidation's consolidation sequence.

Veldmark (fictional): Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly and Keybridge with its March 2027 neutrality commitment, Yardstick, Safe Deal, Valuo, Veldmark ID, the Common Ground program (€140 million), the architecture advice forum, and the cast (Ingrid Halvorsen, Mateus Carvalho, Yara Mendes, Daan Visser, Sven Lindqvist, Tomasz Wiśniewski, Priya Raman, Aisha Rahman, Olivier Petit, Femke).
The failure-pattern names (The Forced Fit, The Copy-Paste Country, Deal-Shaped Architecture, Set-and-Forget AI).
does_not_know: The terms this chapter owns: marketplace team topology and architecture governance.

The inverse Conway maneuver; the four team types and three interaction modes in detail; cognitive load as a design limit; the team API; the decision-rights matrix; the advice process; showback, chargeback, fixed allocation and internal market as funding models.
Common Ground organization v1 and the engineering baseline (158 teams).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an incident that crosses brands, the reader traces it to an ownership defect and names the organizational design that fixes it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A group's largest brand writes a fraud rule in its home country within minutes of an incident. The rule reaches a second country three days later, with a monolith deploy, and never reaches two others, where moderation is run by outsourced vendors; a sister brand never learns that the fraudster's phone number also registered there. Using only this chapter: what is the defect, and what do you change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No team owns trust and safety for the brand or the group; several teams each own a piece. Give the shared trust-and-safety pipeline one platform team that offers it as an internal product with a contract and service level for 'a rule reaches every tenant', keep policy local and mechanism central, cut stream-aligned teams by journey rather than by country, fund policy-driven platforms by fixed allocation so no brand saves by skipping a fraud check, and take the cross-brand decision through the advice process with a record.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Who owns which journey, capability and decision; team types and interaction modes; platform teams as internal products; decision rights, the advice process and funding; the terms marketplace team topology and architecture governance; evidence from documented reorganizations of classifieds groups and the fictional Veldmark's Common Ground organization and advice forum.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

Given a group with one product in several countries and a policy-driven platform, the reader chooses the axis for stream-aligned teams, says when a country team is justified, and picks a funding model for the policy-driven platform with the reason.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand runs the same classifieds product in four countries with a full-stack team per country, and the group is about to charge its brands per moderation decision for a shared trust-and-safety platform. Using only this chapter: how should the brand's teams be cut, when would a country team still be justified, and how should the trust-and-safety platform be funded?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Cut stream-aligned teams by journey within the brand, carrying the country through product roles and configuration; a country team is justified by a different product (such as different sections or fees), not a different language; fund trust and safety by fixed allocation rather than per use, because per-use charging tempts a brand to skip fraud checks.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every statement about a real company carries its date and source, and the reading of Adevinta's reorganizations as Conway's law in reverse is labeled as inference.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Does any claim about a real company lack a date or source, or present inferred internals as fact?
acceptance_criteria.expected: All company claims are dated and sourced; the Adevinta reading sits in an INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED callout.

thesis.question: Which organizational design makes a multi-marketplace architecture work?
thesis.claim: A group of marketplaces builds each shared capability once and gets a fix, such as a fraud rule, into every brand and country within hours rather than days only when every buyer and seller journey, bounded context and shared capability has exactly one owning team within its cognitive load: stream-aligned brand teams cut by journey rather than by country, platform teams that offer shared capabilities as internal products with a published contract, a roadmap and migration help, and specialist teams only for rare subsystems such as ranking and valuation; and when cross-brand decisions are made through an open, recorded advice process under an explicit matrix of what the group, the platforms and each brand decide, rather than by an architecture review board that owns nothing.
thesis.disputed_by: Federated guilds in which brand teams build platforms 'on behalf of the group' and nobody owns them; or a central product-and-technology organization that owns every product and platform, adopted by mandate and deadline and governed by an architecture review board that approves designs.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this reviews the capability map, the context map and the team topology together twice a year and treats any orphaned or split ownership as a defect with a fix and a date; measures each platform team by tenants in production, onboarding cost and remaining shadow copies; funds platform build centrally, then by showback, then by allocation, fixed for policy-driven platforms such as trust and safety; and keeps escalations from the advice forum to about one decision in ten.
thesis.how_why: On 7 March 2027 a phishing rule written by Tradeyard Netherlands reached Belgium on 10 March, with a Yardstick deploy, and never reached Poland or Portugal, whose moderation two outsourced vendors ran; Motorvane never learned that the fraudster's phone number had registered there. Veldmark had about 1,150 engineers in 158 teams, and none of the nine Common Ground capabilities had exactly one owning team. After Common Ground organization v1 (decided 22 June 2027), by December 8 of 9 did, country-cut teams fell from 17 to 4, and cognitive-load flags from 23 to 9; the forum logged 74 cross-brand decisions at a median of nine working days, six escalated to the CTO. Replayed on the shared platform, the rule reached every subscribing tenant within an hour: the rule engine had not changed, the ownership had.

supporting_claims.claim: Ownership is the unit of design: every journey, bounded context and shared capability needs exactly one owning team within its cognitive load, and an incident that reaches markets unevenly is an ownership defect.

Stream-aligned teams are cut by journey within a brand, with countries carried by product roles and configuration; a country team is justified by a different product, not a different language; specialist teams exist only for rare subsystems and own their runtime.

Platform teams earn tenants as internal products with a product owner and tenant-facing roadmap, a contract, self-service onboarding, migration help and cost transparency, funded so that using the platform is a brand's cheapest option: central build, then showback, then usage allocation for cost-driven platforms and fixed allocation for policy-driven ones; mandates without these produce shadow copies.

Cross-brand decisions are made through an open, recorded advice process under an explicit decision-rights matrix, with executive escalation only for money, people and personal data, not by a review board.

role.contribution: Assigns an owning team to every journey, context and shared capability that consolidation moves, and sets the decision rights and forum through which cross-brand decisions are made.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene poses the phishing rule and Mateus's question; worked-example answers them after the body has built the design
trade-offs, verticals, failure-modes, ca-view, questions: the book's standard judging sections

flow.rationale: The scene comes first because its incident and team lists are the problem the chapter solves. Concepts follow because the architecture uses team types, the axis, ownership and governance; placed later, the topology would be described in words the reader cannot yet separate. The architecture comes before the public record so the record has a design to test, and the record comes before Veldmark's worked example so that Veldmark's options can be read against what real groups did; placed before the architecture, the worked example would cite team APIs, matrices and funding models not yet explained. The judging sections apply the whole design, so they come last.

hook.content: Marketplace groups are usually assembled, not designed, and each capability exists as many times as there are teams that believe they own it.

bridge.from_reader_world: Architects of groups built by acquisition know the picture of four identity systems and four trust-and-safety stacks.
bridge.to_topic: The book's shared platforms need owning teams, interaction modes, funding and a way to decide across brands.

thesis_statement.text: Assign one owning team to every journey, context and shared capability; run platforms as internal products that earn tenants; govern with recorded decisions and open advice under explicit decision rights rather than an approval board.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (three bullets), with the WHY callouts and the failure-patterns callout; p01 states the ownership principle and p03 the two terms.

roadmap.placement: Paragraph p04, with the IN THIS CHAPTER callout.

promises.promise: Open with the March 2027 phishing rule and the team lists behind it.
Define the team types and the parts of governance.
Design a topology with platform teams, decision rights, an advice process, funding and the architects who run it.
Test it against what classifieds groups have published.
Follow Veldmark's Common Ground organization through its first year.
Close with trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions to ask.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter owns two terms: a marketplace team topology assigns team types and interaction modes to journeys, bounded contexts and shared capabilities, and architecture governance is the set of decision rights, forums, records, principles and standards through which decisions are made and revisited.

evidence.what: Definitions of marketplace team topology and architecture governance; pointers to bounded-contexts and multi-country-platforms.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the two terms before the scene uses them.

advances_thesis.how: Names the two ideas the thesis is built from.

transition_in.carries_over: Who owns which journey, capability and decision.
transition_in.introduces: The two terms that name the answer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter moves from the March 2027 phishing rule and the team lists behind it to the concepts, a designed topology with decision rights, advice process, funding and the architects who run it, the public record, Veldmark's Common Ground organization in its first year, and the closing trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, Chief Architect's view and questions.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: The Rule That Reached Belgium Three Days Late
sections.controlling_idea: A phishing rule that protected Tradeyard Netherlands within minutes reached Belgium three days late and Poland, Portugal and Motorvane never, because several teams each owned a piece of trust and safety and no team owned the whole.

advances_thesis.how: Poses the chapter's problem as an ownership defect.

flow.rationale: The incident comes first, then its cause in the team lists, then the question the cause raises; the question would make no sense before the reader has seen the split ownership.

transition_in.carries_over: Ownership as the unit of design and the roadmap's first promise, the March 2027 rule.
transition_in.introduces: The incident itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Sunday 7 March 2027 Tradeyard NL's trust-and-safety team handled a fake Safe Deal payment link well: reported at 20:19, account suspended at 20:26, and a new rule withheld 37 similar messages that evening.

evidence.what: Femke's city bike on Tradeyard NL; fake Safe Deal link at 20:11, report 20:19, suspension 20:26, 37 messages withheld.
evidence.shows: Shows the local response worked, so the later failure is not a rule-writing failure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same rule reached Tradeyard Belgium only on Wednesday 10 March with a Yardstick deploy, never reached Poland or Portugal, whose moderation two outsourced vendors ran, and Motorvane never learned the fraudster's phone number had registered there.

evidence.what: Belgium on 10 March via the twice-weekly Yardstick deploy; Poland and Portugal never; the Motorvane private-seller account.
evidence.shows: Shows the same fix reaching each market by a different owner's path.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule worked in the Netherlands.
transition_in.introduces: Its uneven reach everywhere else.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ingrid reads the incident as an organization chart and collects four team lists in four formats, totalling about 1,150 engineers in 158 teams cut in different ways.

evidence.what: Engineers, teams, how teams are cut and architecture function per brand: Tradeyard about 430 (61 teams, about 140 engineers shipping only with Yardstick), Motorvane about 290 (38), Hearthly about 250 (33), Keybridge about 70 (10), group functions about 110 (16); total about 1,150 and 158.
evidence.shows: Shows four organizations cut four ways, with no group owner for shared capabilities.

transition_in.carries_over: The uneven reach of the rule.
transition_in.introduces: Ingrid's reading of it as an organizational, not a trust-and-safety, failure, and the team lists.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The team list explains the incident: trust and safety for Tradeyard was split between an in-house team and two vendors, and the capability map found the same shape in identity, search, catalog and analytics, where several teams each owned a piece and no team owned the whole.

evidence.what: Figure 1: one rule reaching four countries by different paths.
evidence.shows: Shows the four owners behind the four outcomes.

evidence.what: Capability map presented 31 March 2027 (business-capabilities).
evidence.shows: Shows the defect recurs beyond trust and safety.

transition_in.introduces: What it explains: split ownership as the cause.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Mateus Carvalho asks the chapter's question: with €140 million and four years for Common Ground, who will own the shared platforms, who will use them, and who decides when the two disagree?

transition_in.carries_over: No team owned the whole of any shared capability.
transition_in.introduces: The CTO's question about owners, users and decisions.

sections.heading: Concepts: Teams as Part of the Architecture
sections.controlling_idea: Teams are part of the architecture: Conway's law, cognitive load, Team Topologies' four team types and three interaction modes, the axis that cuts stream-aligned teams, ownership of journeys, contexts and capabilities, and the five parts of governance give the vocabulary the design needs.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the terms the design uses.

flow.rationale: Conway and cognitive load justify thinking in teams; the team types are then needed to choose an axis; ownership needs the types; governance comes last because it is how owners decide together. Reversed, the axis would be chosen before the reader knows what a stream-aligned team is.

transition_in.carries_over: Mateus's question about owners, users and decisions.
transition_in.introduces: The observation about teams and systems that starts the answer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Conway's law, read in reverse as the inverse Conway maneuver, is a design tool: to get a shared search platform, create a team whose job is the search platform and give brands a reason to depend on it.

evidence.what: Conway (1968): designs copy communication structures; four brands with four organizations have four identity systems.
evidence.shows: Shows the law holds in a marketplace group, so it can be used deliberately.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The maneuver has two limits: changing teams does not change code, and a team can handle only so much complexity before breaking down.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "Teams can only handle so much complexity before breaking down"; a team owning insertion in four countries, the pro-seller API and the image pipeline.
evidence.shows: Shows why ownership must fit cognitive load.

transition_in.carries_over: The inverse Conway maneuver as a design tool.
transition_in.introduces: Its two limits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Team Topologies' four team types and three interaction modes map onto a listing marketplace with concrete examples.

evidence.what: Stream-aligned, platform, complicated subsystem and enabling teams with marketplace and Veldmark examples.
evidence.shows: Shows each type has a recognizable marketplace counterpart.

evidence.what: Collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitation with when each fits.
evidence.shows: Shows when each mode applies in a marketplace.

transition_in.carries_over: Skelton and Pais's principle on complexity.
transition_in.introduces: Their team types and interaction modes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An interaction mode belongs to a pair of teams at a point in time: collaboration that never ends means the platform has no contract, and X-as-a-Service from day one means it was designed without its tenants.

transition_in.introduces: How modes change over time and what a stuck mode signals.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every marketplace organization must choose the axis that cuts its stream-aligned teams, country, journey or capability layer, and each has a characteristic weakness.

evidence.what: Country, journey and capability-layer teams with strength and weakness.
evidence.shows: Shows country teams rebuild every journey and layer teams own no outcome.

transition_in.introduces: The axis along which those teams are cut.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For one product in several countries, stream-aligned teams should be cut by journey within a brand, with the country carried by product roles and configuration; a country team is justified by a different product, not by a different language.

evidence.what: Tradeyard Poland's vehicles and property sections with insertion fees.
evidence.shows: Shows what a product difference that justifies a market team looks like.

transition_in.carries_over: The weaknesses of country and layer teams.
transition_in.introduces: The recommended axis and its exception.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Across brands the same journey stays separate, because dealer supply and agency supply are different products, and what they share is a platform, not a shared team.

evidence.what: Motorvane dealer supply and Hearthly agency supply; shared supply contract, validator library and taxonomy.
evidence.shows: Shows the shared part is a platform beneath separate journeys.

transition_in.carries_over: One journey team per journey within a brand.
transition_in.introduces: Why journeys are not merged across brands.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ownership is the unit of design: the rule of one owning team per bounded context extends to journeys, contexts and shared capabilities.

transition_in.carries_over: The shared part as a platform with an owner.
transition_in.introduces: Ownership as the unit of design, over three kinds of thing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An owner is the team woken up when the thing breaks, that decides its roadmap and answers for its cost; a consulted team or a committee is never an owner.

transition_in.carries_over: The three kinds of thing to own.
transition_in.introduces: What owning one means.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Architecture governance has five parts, decision rights, decision records, principles, a forum, and standards and golden paths, and review is the least important.

evidence.what: The five parts, what each is and the failure when it is missing.
evidence.shows: Shows that each part prevents a specific failure.

transition_in.carries_over: Owners of journeys, contexts and capabilities.
transition_in.introduces: The chapter's second term: how owners make decisions together.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Nygard's 2011 architecture decision record is still the common shape of a decision record.

evidence.what: Title, context, decision, status, consequences.
evidence.shows: Shows what a record must capture.

transition_in.carries_over: Decision records as one of the five parts.
transition_in.introduces: Their standard format.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Harmel-Law's advice process replaces approval with one rule: anyone may make an architectural decision after seeking advice from those affected and from experts and recording it, supported by records, an open weekly forum, principles and a radar.

evidence.what: "anyone can make an architectural decision"; weekly open architecture advisory forum.
evidence.shows: Shows the governance core the chapter adopts.

transition_in.introduces: The advice process that rests on them.

sections.heading: Architecture: A Topology for a Group of Marketplaces
sections.controlling_idea: A group of marketplaces should stack journey-aligned brand teams on platform teams run as internal products, with specialists and enablers beside them, governed by an explicit decision-rights matrix and an advice process, funded by the reason each platform is shared, and served by few architects placed where decisions are made.

flow.rationale: The whole topology first, then platform teams inside it, then the decision rights, advice process and funding that govern those teams, then the architects who run governance. Funding before decision rights would price platforms nobody has yet been given the right to define.

transition_in.carries_over: The four team types and the five parts of governance.
transition_in.introduces: How they combine into one topology for a group.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Applied to a group of marketplaces, the team types stack: stream-aligned teams per brand and journey on top, platform teams per shared capability beneath, complicated-subsystem teams beside them and enabling teams moving between them. Veldmark's adopted topology is shown as a preview of the decision the worked example tells.

evidence.what: Figure 2: Veldmark's Common Ground team topology (target 2028), introduced as a preview of the June 2027 decision; Keybridge outside the platform organization because of its March 2027 neutrality commitment (it publishes agencies' listings to Hearthly's competitors).
evidence.shows: Shows the layers and who depends on whom.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three properties of the topology matter more than its boxes: dependencies point down through published contracts, specialists serve brands through platforms while brands keep the objective, and enabling teams are temporary by design.

evidence.what: Tradeyard's listing events via a contract; ranking models served through the search platform; the Yardstick Exit team ending by 2029.
evidence.shows: Shows each property in a concrete case.

transition_in.introduces: The three properties that make it work.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform team differs from a shared-services department in five things: a product owner with a tenant-facing roadmap, a contract, self-service onboarding, migration help, and run responsibility with cost transparency.

evidence.what: Each of the five, why it matters and the evidence that it is missing.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader a test for any platform team.

transition_in.introduces: What makes a platform team a product.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adevinta's internal platform is the best-documented classifieds example that voluntary adoption with migration help works, so a mandate belongs only after the platform is clearly cheaper.

evidence.what: Common Platform for about 1,500 engineers in about 20 marketplace companies, voluntary adoption, about ten minutes onboarding, embedded platform engineers (2019 talk, written up January 2020); SCHIP serving more than 4,000 developers by 2023.
evidence.shows: Shows adoption earned with self-service and migration help.

evidence.what: Figure 3: a platform that earns tenants versus a fenced, mandated one.
evidence.shows: Shows mandates produce shadow copies.

transition_in.carries_over: The five things a platform team needs.
transition_in.introduces: The public example of a platform that had them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Governance starts with a decision-rights matrix saying what the group, platform teams, brand engineering and brand product each decide, advise on or are told; Veldmark's matrix serves as the example, introduced with a one-sentence preview of the advice forum (open, weekly, set up in April 2027) that adopted it, which the worked example describes.

evidence.what: Veldmark's matrix adopted April 2027, revised September: sharing, contract, engine, brand features, brand architecture, exceptions, personal data, funding.
evidence.shows: Shows decision rights written down per decision type.

transition_in.introduces: Who decides what among them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The matrix lets brands decide exceptions themselves if they record them, and keeps the decision to share a capability with the CTO after the forum has heard the brands, because it moves money and people.

transition_in.introduces: Its two deliberate features.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Under the advice process most cross-brand decisions stay with the team that proposes them, and only those moving funding, people or personal data go to an accountable executive.

evidence.what: Figure 4: the advice process applied to cross-brand decisions.
evidence.shows: Shows the path and the narrow escalation.

transition_in.carries_over: Exceptions decided by brands and sharing decided by the CTO.
transition_in.introduces: The path a cross-brand decision takes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The advice process gives up approval but keeps public advice, recorded decisions and a review date or trigger on every record.

evidence.what: Figure 5: review board queue versus open advice forum.
evidence.shows: Shows why a board is routed around and the forum is not.

transition_in.introduces: What it keeps in place of approval.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Funding shapes platform behavior more than any principle, and each of five common models produces different behavior.

evidence.what: Central program budget, fixed allocation, showback, chargeback by usage, internal market, with behavior and fit.
evidence.shows: Shows each model's incentive.

transition_in.introduces: Funding, which shapes behavior more.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Funding should be chosen per platform by why it is shared: policy-driven platforms such as trust and safety and identity should not be charged per use, while cost-driven ones such as search and media should.

evidence.what: Charging per decision would tempt a brand to skip checks.
evidence.shows: Shows why per-use charging breaks policy-driven platforms.

transition_in.introduces: Picking one per platform rather than one for all.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Cost attribution needs an ownership catalog before it needs a pricing model.

evidence.what: Adevinta cloud governance, December 2024: "You build it, you run it (and you pay for it)", ownership catalog of more than a thousand cloud accounts and projects.
evidence.shows: Shows attribution rests on mapped ownership.

transition_in.carries_over: Usage pricing that makes cost visible.
transition_in.introduces: What it requires first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A marketplace group needs fewer architects than it thinks, placed where decisions are made, each role owning some things and not others.

evidence.what: Group Chief Architect, brand lead architect, platform architect, principal engineers: owns and does not own.
evidence.shows: Shows no architect role owns an approval gate.

transition_in.carries_over: Ownership mapped to teams and costs.
transition_in.introduces: The roles architects play in this design.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An architect should never make a decision the team can make on its own, as a 2018 Berlin Tech Blog post put it, a description of the role that has aged well.

evidence.what: "A Software Architect should never make a decision that the team can effectively make on their own" (eBay Kleinanzeigen and mobile.de, 2018), marked as old evidence.
evidence.shows: Supports architects advising rather than approving.

transition_in.introduces: Public support for the rule behind them.

sections.heading: In Practice: What the Public Record Shows
sections.controlling_idea: The public record of classifieds groups supports the design only in fragments: journey-aligned teams, domain maps before reorganizations, platforms that grew by adoption and specialists owning their runtime, and no group has published a complete topology.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the design against dated public evidence.

flow.rationale: One company per paragraph, from the journey axis (Marktplaats) and ownership before reorganization (Vinted, AutoScout24) to cross-cutting governance and specialists (OLX) and whole-group swings (Adevinta, eCG), then the common thread; the companies go from the narrowest claim (one axis at one company) to the widest (whole-group swings), so each fragment adds a level, and the summary must come last because it draws on all fragments.

transition_in.carries_over: The design as the author's recommendation.
transition_in.introduces: What real classifieds groups have published, and how little that is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Few marketplace groups publish their organization designs, so each dated fragment is evidence about one organization at one time.
Marktplaats's 2017 move from business-unit teams to journey teams is the clearest classifieds account of cutting teams by journey, with the architecture following the teams.

evidence.what: November 2017: Journey Teams, OKRs (at most three objectives, four key results), self-reported "10x faster"; nine years old.
evidence.shows: Supports the journey axis.

transition_in.introduces: The first: Marktplaats.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vinted mapped almost 300 domains over at least two years before restructuring teams, so the domain map came before the team change and both before the services.

evidence.what: "It took us at least two years to understand the domains, as we identified almost 300 of them" (January 2026).
evidence.shows: Supports mapping ownership before reorganizing.

transition_in.introduces: Vinted's order: domains, then teams.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: AutoScout24 staffed its migration by growing a new organization from one team to eight rather than reassigning the old one in one move.

evidence.what: Project Tatsu, began November 2014, one to eight teams, a team every two to three months (2016 report).
evidence.shows: Supports moving people as work moves.

transition_in.introduces: Growing the new organization gradually.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: OLX shows that journey squads alone do not deliver cross-cutting hygiene and that a lightweight, outcome-tracked structure for cross-team initiatives is a governance tool.

sections.heading: Veldmark Worked Example: The Common Ground Organization Design
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark answers Mateus's question with Common Ground organization v1, a central product-run platform organization with journey-aligned brand teams, team APIs, phased funding and an open advice forum, and in its first year owned capabilities rose to 8 of 9 and the March rule could reach every subscribing tenant within an hour.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the whole design and measures it.

flow.rationale: The decision comes first (options in May, Common Ground organization v1 in June with its year-end measures after its five parts), then the parts that make it work in the order a tenant meets them (team API and collaboration limit, funding and its exception), then the forum that advised on all of them, with its month-by-month log, year-end totals and principles, then the November replay as the test of the scene's problem. The forum is previewed in one sentence in the Architecture section, so the options can be put to it before its own subsection; placed first, its log listed the June decision before the May options (round 3, both flow readers). The replay must come last because it relies on the owner, the forum and the block-list decision.

transition_in.carries_over: The design and the public fragments.
transition_in.introduces: Veldmark applying the design to Mateus's question: the options put to its advice forum.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark answered Mateus's question through its architecture advice forum: in May 2027 Ingrid and Yara Mendes put three options to the forum, whose twelve principles include 'share platforms, not products': federated guilds, a central product-run platform organization, and central product and technology.

evidence.what: Options A, B, C with for and against.
evidence.shows: Shows why guilds keep the current defect and full centralization breaks 'share platforms, not products'.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On the forum's advice Mateus decided option B on 22 June 2027, effective 1 September, as Common Ground organization v1 in five parts; a callout after the parts names the nine capabilities the board's January 2027 program set out and reports that by December 2027 eight had one owner, while country-cut, overloaded and Yardstick-bound teams had fallen.

evidence.what: Five parts: one owning team per capability under Yara Mendes (Data & ML with Priya Raman); brands keep journey teams, Tradeyard PL/PT country teams become journey teams, one PL market team; policy local, mechanism central (Aisha Rahman); people move with work, about 150 transferred and 80 hired, about 230 engineers in 24 teams; Keybridge outside.
evidence.shows: Shows the design as a dated decision.

evidence.what: BY DECEMBER 2027 callout before the table: the nine program capabilities named (Veldmark ID, trust and safety, media, search, messaging, catalog and entitlements, event backbone, data platform, taxonomy and attributes; part 1 adds the listing and developer platforms), eight single-owned.
evidence.shows: Explains the table and reconciles the nine with the platforms in part 1.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md, Common Ground program line (Veldmark is fictional)

evidence.what: March versus December 2027: engineers 1,150 to 1,200, teams 158 to 152, owned capabilities 0 to 8 of 9, Yardstick-bound teams 19 to 14, country-cut 17 to 4, cognitive-load flags 23 to 9.
evidence.shows: Shows the ownership defect measurably reduced.

transition_in.introduces: The forum's advice and the decision.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each platform team publishes a one-page team API, and the search platform's page shows honestly that in its first year it has no steady-state tenant.

evidence.what: Search platform, second half of 2027: collaboration with Tradeyard Portugal, facilitation with Motorvane (Listing Search API v1 on Elasticsearch), X-as-a-Service with nobody yet.
evidence.shows: Shows interaction modes recorded per tenant.

transition_in.introduces: How each owner presents itself to tenants.

evidence.what: Two quarters per tenant; the forum's question when the box runs out.
evidence.shows: Shows collaboration ending in a contract rather than continuing indefinitely.

transition_in.carries_over: Collaboration modes on the team API.
transition_in.introduces: The limit on collaboration.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The decision record funds platforms by phase: Common Ground pays for the build in 2027 and 2028, showback per tenant from Q1 2028, and from 2029 usage allocation for cost-driven platforms and fixed allocation for policy-driven ones.

evidence.what: Units per thousand searches, per million events, per thousand stored images, per moderation decision.
evidence.shows: Shows the funding models applied by phase and by reason for sharing.

transition_in.carries_over: The decision record's ownership and collaboration rules.
transition_in.introduces: Its funding rules.

evidence.what: Olivier Petit's condition; Motorvane Q1 2028, Tradeyard Q2 2028.
evidence.shows: Shows funding adjusted to migration risk.

transition_in.introduces: One exception.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The forum that advised on these decisions was set up in April 2027 as a weekly, open, one-hour meeting with mandatory decision records for cross-brand decisions, and its first year can be read from its log.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four of Veldmark's twelve principles do most of the work, each with a test and a decision it shaped.

evidence.what: Share platforms not products; one owner per context and capability; contracts before migrations; separable by tenant.
evidence.shows: Shows principles as testable rules, not slogans.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The separability principle comes from Veldmark's private-equity ownership, since a brand may be sold and unwinding a shared platform is costly.

transition_in.introduces: Why the fourth exists.

evidence.shows: Shows the scene's defect fixed by ownership.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: The Chief Architect designs ownership on the same map as the architecture, measures platforms by adoption and tenant cost, keeps the forum open and escalations few, expects the pendulum, and watches named signals.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the design into the Chief Architect's decisions.

flow.rationale: Ownership first because every other decision assumes owners; measuring the platform owners next, because they are the new teams; then governance among them, then the long view that outlasts any one structure; who-decides-and-what-to-watch closes because it summarizes the others. Measurement placed before ownership would measure teams nobody has yet named.

transition_in.introduces: The decisions that prevent them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Design ownership first and draw it on the same map as the capabilities and contexts, reviewing the three twice a year and treating any orphan or split ownership as a defect with a fix and date.
Measure platforms by adoption and tenant cost, not output: tenants in production, onboarding cost, shadow copies and the share of roadmap from tenants.

transition_in.introduces: How to measure the platform owners.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Keep the forum open and executive decisions few; if more than about one decision in ten escalates, the decision rights are wrong.

transition_in.introduces: Keeping governance light.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Expect the pendulum between centralization and decentralization, so separability and platform contracts, not team structures, are the durable assets.

transition_in.introduces: The longer-term swing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The CTO decides topology and funding on the forum's advice, the Chief Architect owns principles, matrix and maps, platform heads own contracts and brand leaders own journeys, and six signals show whether it works.

conclusion.heading: From Organization to Migration
conclusion.synthesis: Mateus's question has a three-part answer that works only as a whole: platform teams own shared capabilities and earn brands as tenants, journey teams use them, and disagreements are decided by the proposing team after public advice under a matrix that escalates only money, people and personal data; without owners the forum has nobody to advise, and without the forum and funding the owners have no tenants.
conclusion.so_what: With this organization a capability exists once because one team owns it, and a fix such as a fraud rule reaches every subscribing tenant within an hour instead of days.

callback.to: The scene's March 2027 phishing rule and Mateus's question (who will own, who will use, who decides).
callback.how: The reader sees the same rule engine reaching every subscribing tenant once one team owns the outcome, and the question answered part by part.

takeaway.content: Draw the team topology on the capability and context maps, give every orphaned or split capability one owner, write the decision-rights matrix and start an open forum with recorded decisions.

hand_off.carries_over: The organization assigns owners but does not move code; Tradeyard's teams still deploy through Yardstick, and the new platform teams own capabilities the monolith still implements.
hand_off.introduces: Moving a live marketplace from the old system to the new one without losing traffic, sellers or revenue.
